In natural language processing, a word embedding is a representation of a word. The embedding is used in text analysis. Typically, the representation is a real-valued vector that encodes the meaning of the word in such a way that the words that are closer in the vector space are expected to be similar in meaning. Word embeddings can be obtained using language modeling and feature learning techniques, where words or phrases from the vocabulary are mapped to vectors of real numbers.
Methods to generate this mapping include neural networks, dimensionality reduction on the word co-occurrence matrix, probabilistic models, explainable knowledge base method, and explicit representation in terms of the context in which words appear.
Word and phrase embeddings, when used as the underlying input representation, have been shown to boost the performance in NLP tasks such as syntactic parsing and sentiment analysis.

In information retrieval, Okapi BM25 (BM is an abbreviation of best matching) is a ranking function used by search engines to estimate the relevance of documents to a given search query. It is based on the probabilistic retrieval framework developed in the 1970s and 1980s by Stephen E. Robertson, Karen Spärck Jones, and others.
The name of the actual ranking function is BM25. The fuller name, Okapi BM25, includes the name of the first system to use it, which was the Okapi information retrieval system, implemented at London's City University in the 1980s and 1990s. BM25 and its newer variants, e.g. BM25F (a version of BM25 that can take document structure and anchor text into account), represent TF-IDF-like retrieval functions used in document retrieval.

Idf was introduced as "term specificity" by Karen Spärck Jones in a 1972 paper. Although it has worked well as a heuristic, its theoretical foundations have been troublesome for at least three decades afterward, with many researchers trying to find information theoretic justifications for it.

Personal data is any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (“data subject”) — that is, any data that can identify a person directly or indirectly by reference to an identifier such as a name, identification number, location data, online identifier, or any factor specific to the person’s physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity [3][4].

Specific categories expressly recognised as personal data include genetic data (information about inherited or acquired genetic characteristics) and biometric data (information resulting from technical processing of physical, physiological or behavioural characteristics that allow unique identification) [2].  

Online identifiers such as IP addresses, cookie IDs or RFID tags can also constitute personal data when they can be combined with other information to create a profile that identifies the natural person [5].

In economics, inflation is an increase in the average price of goods and services in terms of money, though it originally referred to the increase of the money supply (monetary inflation) that can cause such a universal shift. This increase is measured using a price index, typically a consumer price index (CPI). When the general price level rises, each unit of currency buys fewer goods and services; consequently, inflation corresponds to a reduction in the purchasing power of money. The opposite of inflation is deflation, a decrease in the general price level of goods and services. The common measure of inflation is the inflation rate, the annualized percentage change in a general price index.

sum-wb.question: Summarize the World Bank's 2024 annual report.
sum-wb.answer: The World Bank’s 2024 Annual Report highlights a broad push to “enable prosperity through jobs, tax policy, economic policy, financial inclusion, and small‑business support” and notes a new review with the IMF of the Debt Sustainability Framework for low‑income countries to spot debt risks early [1]. In the first half of fiscal 2024 the Bank helped feed 156 million people, improved schooling for 280 million students, provided water, sanitation or hygiene to 59 million, reached 287 million people with social‑protection support, enabled sustainable transport for 77 million, and added 17 GW of renewable‑energy capacity, while committing to devote 45 % of annual financing to climate action by 2025, split evenly between mitigation and adaptation [2][4]. Digital transformation was a priority, with a record 53 active digital‑lending projects totaling $5.6 billion, the launch of a dedicated Digital Vice‑Presidency, and the inaugural Global Digital Summit to explore opportunities and risks [3]. The Bank identified eight global challenges—climate change, fragility and conflict, pandemic preparedness, energy access, food and nutrition security, water security, enabling digitalization, and protecting biodiversity—to guide its strategy, delivering systematic country diagnostics, partnership frameworks, and performance reviews, and introduced new financial instruments that will free $40 billion over ten years by adjusting its loan‑to‑equity ratio [5][6]. The President’s message underscores a looming jobs gap: 1.2 billion young people in the Global South will reach working age in the next decade, yet only 424 million jobs are projected, prompting urgent efforts to create opportunities and launch at least 15 country‑led methane‑reduction programs by fiscal 2026 [4].
